questions.question: Explain the difference between population distribution and population density, and use an example to show why the two can never substitute for each other in an answer.
questions.expected_answer: Population distribution is the pattern of where people are found across an area, described in words such as even, uneven, clustered, linear, dispersed, dense or sparse — a word-picture of the map. Population density is a number: total population divided by total area, expressed as people per square kilometre, measuring crowding rather than arrangement. The two are independent: two wards of 1 200 square kilometres each holding 72 000 people both have a density of 60 people per square kilometre, yet one may have its people spread evenly across smallholdings while the other packs every resident into a single fishing town in one corner with the rest empty. Identical density, opposite distributions. The number answers how many; the pattern answers where — so a density figure can never describe a pattern, and a pattern description can never replace the calculation. Density is also an average, so a figure like South Africa's fifty-odd people per square kilometre buries the extremes it is built from and describes no actual place.

questions.question: Describe the physical factors that shape population distribution, giving a named example for each of where it attracts settlement and where it repels it.
questions.expected_answer: RELIEF: level or gently rolling land attracts ploughing, building and roads, while steep broken terrain such as the high interior of Lesotho and the Drakensberg escarpment repels settlement through thin soils, difficult access and costly construction; in hot latitudes altitude can attract because highland air is cooler and healthier. CLIMATE is the strongest control: moderate temperatures and reliable rain underlie the world's population belts, while the Namib and Sahara repel through drought, Siberia and the polar fringe through a frozen growing season, and the Congo basin rainforest through leached soils, dense growth and disease. WATER SUPPLY: settlement gathers at rivers, springs and dependable groundwater — ancient dense populations line the Nile and Ganges, and arid regions show linear threads of villages tracing a river. SOILS: the volcanic soils of Java and the delta silts of Bangladesh feed dense rural populations, while sandy, thin or saline soils carry few people. NATURAL RESOURCES: a mineral deposit is fixed, so people must come to it, planting settlement in otherwise repellent places. VEGETATION AND DISEASE: dense forest obstructs settlement, and diseases such as malaria historically kept farmers out of low-lying African valleys. ACCESSIBILITY: natural harbours, navigable rivers and easy passes concentrate trade and therefore people.

questions.question: Describe and explain South Africa's population distribution, making sure your answer covers physical causes, economic causes and historical causes.
questions.expected_answer: The pattern is sharply uneven. Physically, a moisture divide splits the country: the east, with annual rainfall above roughly 500 millimetres, is comparatively well settled, while the dry western two-fifths — the Karoo, Bushmanland, the Kalahari margins and Namaqualand — are sparse, with huge farms and settlement clustered at water points and mining towns. Economically, four urban concentrations dominate. Gauteng is the largest and the anomaly: an inland province with no harbour or navigable river, it holds about a quarter of the population on under two percent of the land because the Witwatersrand gold discovery of the 1880s summoned workers, then supplying industries, then finance, and the concentration outlived the gold because established jobs, roads and people hold one another in place. The Durban region grew on the country's busiest harbour, Cape Town on the oldest anchorage and now services, tourism and administration, and the Gqeberha-East London coast on harbours and vehicle manufacturing; newer centres such as Richards Bay show the same job-driven chain. Historically, remarkably high rural densities occur in the former homeland territories — areas such as QwaQwa, Venda and Gazankulu in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo — where apartheid legislation compressed the majority of the population onto a fraction of the land; these densities are a political inheritance the farmland cannot support, and they continue to drive migration to the cities.
